title: Experiments, Outcomes and Probability
seo_title: Grade 7 Experiments and Outcomes Worksheets with Answers (MATATAG Math 7)
standard_text: Collect data from experiments (e.g., number of heads obtained when tossing a coin a number of times, number of prime numbers obtained when rolling a die a number of times); express outcomes in words and/or symbols, and represent outcomes in tables and/or graphs; solve problems using the outcomes of experiments.
meta_desc: Free Grade 7 probability worksheets for the DepEd MATATAG curriculum: experiments, outcomes, sample spaces, theoretical and experimental probability. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: More trials: experimental probability gets closer to theoretical.
body_html:
How to think about it

  • An experiment is an activity with results we can observe, like tossing a coin. Each result is an outcome. All the outcomes form the sample space.
  • Outcomes can be written in words, as lists like {H, T}, or in tables and tree diagrams.
  • Theoretical probability = number of favorable outcomes ÷ number of possible outcomes. Rolling a prime on a die: {2, 3, 5}, so 3 ÷ 6 = 12.
  • Experimental probability = number of times it happened ÷ number of trials. With more trials, it usually gets closer to the theoretical probability.

Examples

Example

A coin lands heads 23 times in 40 tosses

23 ÷ 40

Answer: experimental probability 0.575

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Missing outcomesUse a table or tree diagram to list them all.
Upside downFavorable outcomes go on top.
Expecting an exact matchExperiments vary; more trials get closer.

faq.q: What does MATATAG Math 7 ask about probability?
faq.a: Collect data from experiments, express outcomes in words and/or symbols and represent them in tables and/or graphs, and solve problems using the outcomes of experiments.

faq.q: What is the sample space of tossing two coins?
Can a probability be more than 1?
Why do experimental results differ from the theory?
faq.a: Because of chance; the difference usually shrinks with more trials.

items.q: You toss a coin and spin a spinner with 2 equal sections, red and blue. Which list shows all the outcomes? (H = heads, T = tails, R = red, B = blue)
items.e: Pair each coin face with each color: 2 × 2 = 4 outcomes, HR, HB, TR, TB. H, T, R, B lists single results, not pairs. HT is not possible: there is only one coin.

items.q: You toss two coins. Which list shows the whole sample space?
items.e: The first coin can be H or T, and so can the second: 2 × 2 = 4 outcomes, HH, HT, TH, TT. HT and TH are different: heads on the first coin is not the same as heads on the second.

items.q: How many outcomes does the tree diagram show?
items.e: Each of the 2 coin branches splits into 3 colors: 2 × 3 = 6 outcomes. 5 comes from adding 2 + 3.

items.q: Which outcome is NOT in the sample space?
items.e: The spinner only has red, blue and yellow, so H, green can’t happen. The other three are all at the end of a branch.

items.q: How many branches come out of H?
items.e: After heads, the spinner can land on 1, 2, 3 or 4, so 4 branches come out of H. 8 is the number of outcomes in the whole tree.

items.q: How many outcomes in the table show tails?
items.e: The tails row has T1, T2, T3, T4, T5 and T6: 6 outcomes. 12 is the whole table.

items.q: How many outcomes show heads and an odd number?
items.e: Heads and odd: H1, H3 and H5, so 3 outcomes. 6 counts the odd numbers with tails too.

items.q: How many outcomes show a 6?
items.e: A 6 can come with heads or with tails: H6 and T6, so 2 outcomes. 1 forgets that the coin can land either way.

items.q: You toss a coin and roll a number cube with the numbers 1 to 6. How many outcomes are there?
items.e: Each coin face goes with each of the 6 numbers: 2 × 6 = 12. 8 comes from adding 2 + 6.

items.q: You spin spinner A and spinner B. How many outcomes are there?
items.e: Each color goes with each of the 4 numbers: 2 × 4 = 8. 6 comes from adding 2 + 4.

items.q: Which list shows every outcome with blue? (R = red, B = blue)
items.e: Blue on spinner A can go with any of the 4 numbers on spinner B: B1, B2, B3, B4.

items.q: You toss a coin and spin a spinner with 5 equal sections numbered 1 to 5. How many outcomes are there?
items.e: 2 coin faces × 5 numbers = 10 outcomes. 7 comes from 2 + 5. 25 is 5 × 5, as if there were two spinners.

items.q: You spin a spinner with 3 equal sections (red, blue and yellow) two times. How many outcomes are there?
items.e: Each of the 3 colors on the first spin goes with each of the 3 colors on the second: 3 × 3 = 9. 6 comes from adding 3 + 3.

items.q: You roll two number cubes, each with the numbers 1 to 6. How many outcomes are there?
items.e: Each of the 6 numbers on the first cube goes with each of the 6 on the second: 6 × 6 = 36. 12 comes from adding 6 + 6. 11 is the number of different sums (2 to 12), not outcomes.

items.q: The table shows the sum for every outcome of rolling two number cubes. How many outcomes give a sum of 7?
items.e: The 7s run along a diagonal: 1 + 6, 2 + 5, 3 + 4, 4 + 3, 5 + 2, 6 + 1. That is 6 outcomes. 3 forgets that 1 + 6 and 6 + 1 is different outcomes.

items.q: How many outcomes give a sum of 10?
items.e: 4 + 6, 5 + 5 and 6 + 4: 3 outcomes. 2 forgets that 4 + 6 and 6 + 4 are different.

items.q: Which probability best describes an event that is impossible?
items.e: Probability goes from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). 1/2 means equally likely. Near 0 is unlikely and near 1 is likely.

items.q: Which probability best describes an event that is certain?
items.e: Probability goes from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). 1/2 means equally likely. Near 0 is unlikely and near 1 is likely.

items.q: Which probability best describes an event that is equally likely as not?
items.e: Probability goes from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). 1/2 means equally likely. Near 0 is unlikely and near 1 is likely.

items.q: Which probability best describes an event that is unlikely?
items.e: Probability goes from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). 1/2 means equally likely. Near 0 is unlikely and near 1 is likely.

items.q: The spinner has equal sections. What is the probability of landing on red?
items.e: 2 of the 4 equal sections are red, so P(red) = 2/4 = 1/2.

items.q: The spinner has equal sections. What is the probability of landing on blue?
items.e: 3 of the 6 equal sections are blue, so P(blue) = 3/6 = 1/2.

items.q: The spinner has equal sections. What is the probability of landing on red?
items.e: 4 of the 8 equal sections are red, so P(red) = 4/8 = 1/2.

items.q: The spinner has equal sections. What is the probability of landing on yellow?
items.e: 1 of the 5 equal sections are yellow, so P(yellow) = 1/5. Not 1/4: divide by all 5 sections, not just the sections that are not yellow.

items.q: The spinner has equal sections. What is the probability of landing on blue?
items.e: 2 of the 6 equal sections are blue, so P(blue) = 2/6 = 1/3. Not 1/2: divide by all 6 sections, not just the sections that are not blue.

items.q: The spinner has equal sections. What is the probability of landing on green?
items.e: 3 of the 8 equal sections are green, so P(green) = 3/8. Not 3/5: divide by all 8 sections, not just the sections that are not green.

items.q: You pick one marble without looking. What is the probability it is red?
items.e: There are 3 red marbles out of 8 in all. P(red) = 3/8.

items.q: You pick one marble without looking. What is the probability it is green?
items.e: There are 4 green marbles out of 12 in all. P(green) = 4/12 = 1/3.

items.q: You pick one marble without looking. What is the probability it is green?
items.e: There are 6 green marbles out of 10 in all. P(green) = 6/10 = 3/5.

items.q: You pick one marble without looking. What is the probability it is yellow?
items.e: There are 3 yellow marbles out of 10 in all. P(yellow) = 3/10.

items.q: You roll a fair number cube with faces 1 to 6. What is P(a 4)?
items.e: 1 of the 6 faces works, so the probability is 1/6.

items.q: You roll a fair number cube with faces 1 to 6. What is P(an even number)?
items.e: 3 of the 6 faces work, so the probability is 3/6 = 1/2.

items.q: You roll a fair number cube with faces 1 to 6. What is P(a number greater than 4)?
items.e: 2 of the 6 faces work, so the probability is 2/6 = 1/3.

items.q: You roll a fair number cube with faces 1 to 6. What is P(a number less than 3)?
items.e: 2 of the 6 faces work, so the probability is 2/6 = 1/3.

items.q: You roll a fair number cube with faces 1 to 6. What is P(a multiple of 3)?
items.e: 2 of the 6 faces work, so the probability is 2/6 = 1/3.

items.q: You roll a fair number cube with faces 1 to 6. What is P(a prime number (2, 3 or 5))?
items.e: 3 of the 6 faces work, so the probability is 3/6 = 1/2.

items.q: Each letter of the word MISSISSIPPI is on its own card. You pick one card. What is P(S)?
items.e: There are 11 letters and 4 of them are S. P(S) = 4/11.

items.q: A class has 12 girls and 15 boys. The teacher picks one student at random. What is P(girl)?
items.e: 12 girls out of 27 learners: 12/27 = 4/9. Not 4/5 (12/15): divide by all 27 learners.

items.q: A month has 30 days. One day is picked at random. What is the probability that it is the 15th?
items.e: Only 1 of the 30 days works: 1/30.

items.q: A jar has 10 cards numbered 1 to 10. What is P(a number greater than 7)?
items.e: 8, 9 and 10 work: 3 out of 10 = 3/10.

items.q: What is the experimental probability of HH, as a decimal?
items.e: HH came up 12 times in 50 tosses: 1250 = 24100 = 0.24. 0.25 is the theoretical probability. 0.12 uses the count as the decimal.

items.q: What is the experimental probability of one head and one tail, as a decimal?
items.e: One head and one tail is HT or TH: 13 + 14 = 27 times. 2750 = 54100 = 0.54. 0.5 is the theoretical probability.

items.q: What is the experimental probability of TT, as a percent?
items.e: TT came up 11 times in 50: 1150 = 22100 = 22%. 11% uses the count as the percent. 78% is NOT TT.

items.q: Which outcome has an experimental probability of 0.28?
items.e: 0.28 = 28100 = 1450. TH came up 14 times, so the answer is TH.

items.q: Jomar tosses a coin and rolls a number cube 60 times. He gets heads and a 6 four times. What is the experimental probability of heads and a 6?
items.e: Experimental probability = times it happened ÷ number of trials = 460. 112 is the theoretical probability. 456 compares with the other trials, not with all 60.

items.q: Isabel rolls two number cubes 90 times. The sum is 7 on 18 rolls. What is the experimental probability of a sum of 7?
items.e: 1890 = 15. 16 is the theoretical probability, not what happened. 1872 divides by the rolls that were not 7.

items.q: What is the experimental probability of blue, 2 as a percent?
items.e: Blue, 2 came up 14 times in 40 spins: 1440 = 35100 = 35%. 14% uses the count as the percent. 25% is the theory.

items.q: What is the experimental probability of blue with either number, as a decimal?
items.e: Blue, 1 and blue, 2: 6 + 14 = 20 times. 2040 = 0.5. 0.35 uses only blue, 2, and 0.15 only blue, 1.

items.q: What is the experimental probability of a 1 with either color, as a decimal?
items.e: Red, 1 and blue, 1: 11 + 6 = 17 times. 1740 = 17 ÷ 40 = 0.425. 0.275 uses only red, 1. 0.5 is the theory.

items.q: What is the experimental probability of H, yellow as a percent?
items.e: H, yellow came up 12 times in 60: 1260 = 15 = 20%. About 17% is the theory (16). 12% uses the count as the percent.

items.q: What is the experimental probability of red, with either heads or tails?
items.e: H, red and T, red: 11 + 8 = 19 times in 60 trials: 1960. 1941 compares red with the other results, not with all 60.

items.q: Which outcome has an experimental probability of 0.15?
items.e: 0.15 × 60 = 9. H, blue came up 9 times: 960 = 0.15.

items.q: After 50 trials, the experimental probability of heads and an even number is 0.3. How many times did heads and an even number happen?
items.e: 0.3 × 50 = 15. Check: 1550 = 310 = 0.3. 35 is the number of trials when it did NOT happen.

items.q: Bea tosses a coin and rolls a number cube 60 times. She gets heads and an even number 18 times. What is the experimental probability, as a percent?
items.e: 1860 = 310 = 30%. 25% is the theory. 18% uses the count as the percent.

items.q: Jericho tosses a coin 60 times and gets heads 33 times. What is the experimental probability of heads?
items.e: Experimental probability = times it happened ÷ number of trials = 33 ÷ 60 = 1120. (The theoretical probability is 12.)

items.q: Rica rolls a die 72 times. A prime number (2, 3 or 5) comes up 44 times. How many times would you expect a prime number in theory?
items.e: P(prime) = 36 = 12. 12 × 72 = 36 times. The actual result, 44, is close but not exact.

items.q: Ella tosses a coin 80 times and gets heads 43 times. What is the experimental probability of heads?
items.e: Experimental probability = times it happened ÷ number of trials = 43 ÷ 80 = 4380. (The theoretical probability is 12.)

items.q: Miguel rolls a die 48 times. A prime number (2, 3 or 5) comes up 23 times. How many times would you expect a prime number in theory?
items.e: P(prime) = 36 = 12. 12 × 48 = 24 times. The actual result, 23, is close but not exact.

items.q: Ella tosses a coin 40 times and gets heads 19 times. What is the experimental probability of heads?
items.e: Experimental probability = times it happened ÷ number of trials = 19 ÷ 40 = 1940. (The theoretical probability is 12.)

items.q: Kevin tosses a coin 100 times and gets heads 52 times. What is the experimental probability of heads?
items.e: Experimental probability = times it happened ÷ number of trials = 52 ÷ 100 = 1325. (The theoretical probability is 12.)

items.q: A coin was flipped 50 times and landed on heads 28 times. What is the experimental probability of heads?
items.e: Experimental probability = times it happened ÷ total tries = 28/50 = 14/25.

items.q: A number cube was rolled 60 times. It showed 3 twelve times. What is the experimental probability of rolling a 3?
items.e: Experimental probability = times it happened ÷ total tries = 12/60 = 1/5.

items.q: A spinner was spun 40 times and landed on blue 14 times. What is the experimental probability of blue?
items.e: Experimental probability = times it happened ÷ total tries = 14/40 = 7/20.

items.q: A basketball player made 18 of 25 shots. What is the experimental probability of making a shot?
items.e: Experimental probability = times it happened ÷ total tries = 18/25 = 18/25.

items.q: Out of 80 cars that passed, 32 were white. What is the experimental probability of a white car?
items.e: Experimental probability = times it happened ÷ total tries = 32/80 = 2/5.

items.q: The probability of rolling a 5 is 1/6. You roll a number cube 120 times. About how many times should you expect a 5?
items.e: Multiply the probability by the number of tries. 1/6 × 120 = 20.

items.q: A spinner lands on red with probability 1/4. It is spun 200 times. About how many times will it land on red?
items.e: Multiply the probability by the number of tries. 1/4 × 200 = 50.

items.q: A player makes 70% of free throws. About how many will she make in 40 tries?
items.e: Multiply the probability by the number of tries. 0.7 × 40 = 28.

items.q: The probability a light bulb is broken is 0.02. About how many broken bulbs are in a box of 500?
items.e: Multiply the probability by the number of tries. 0.02 × 500 = 10.

items.q: A coin is flipped 300 times. About how many heads do you expect?
items.e: Multiply the probability by the number of tries. 1/2 × 300 = 150.

items.q: Out of 50 learners surveyed, 15 walk to school. A school has 600 learners. About how many walk to school?
items.e: Multiply the probability by the number of tries. 15/50 = 0.3, and 0.3 × 600 = 180.

items.q: A coin is flipped 10 times and lands on heads 7 times. What does this show?
c: The next flip will be tails.
The theoretical probability of heads is 7/10.
Experimental results can differ from the theoretical probability of 1/2.
items.e: With only 10 flips, results vary a lot. With many more flips, the fraction of heads usually gets closer to 1/2.

items.q: Which is most likely to give an experimental probability close to the theoretical probability?
items.e: More trials usually bring the experimental probability closer to the theoretical probability.

items.q: A spinner was spun 100 times: red 48, blue 27, green 25. Which spinner is most likely?
c: Red covers about half; blue and green about a quarter each.
items.e: 48/100 is close to 1/2, and 27/100 and 25/100 are close to 1/4.

items.q: A spinner landed on yellow 9 times in 30 spins. Based on this, what is the probability of yellow?
items.e: 9/30 = 3/10. Not 9/21: divide by all 30 spins.

items.q: A bag has 2 red and 8 blue marbles. You pick and replace a marble 50 times. About how many reds should you expect?
Theoretical P(green) = 1/3. In 60 spins, green came up 26 times. Which is true?
c: Green came up more than expected (20).
Green came up less than expected.
Green came up exactly as expected.
items.e: Expected: 1/3 × 60 = 20. 26 is more than 20.

items.q: A survey found that 12 of 40 people like jazz best. What is the experimental probability that a person likes jazz best?
Two number cubes are rolled 36 times. A sum of 7 came up 8 times. The theoretical probability is 6/36. Which is true?
c: The experimental probability (8/36) is a little higher than 6/36.
items.e: 8/36 is a little more than 6/36. Small differences are normal in experiments.

items.q: A spinner has 4 equal sections, 1 of them green. Ana spins it 80 times. About how many times should it land on green?
You toss a coin and roll a number cube 120 times. About how many times would you expect heads and a 6?
items.e: Heads and 6 is 112. 112 of 120 = 120 ÷ 12 = about 10. About 15 comes from 120 ÷ 8 (adding 2 + 6 outcomes). About 20 uses 16 only.

items.q: You toss two coins 200 times. About how many times would you expect two heads?
items.e: P(HH) = 14. 14 of 200 = about 50. About 67 uses 13, which forgets that HT and TH are different.

items.q: You roll two number cubes 360 times. About how many times would you expect a sum of 7?
items.e: P(sum of 7) = 636 = 16. 360 ÷ 6 = about 60. About 33 treats the 11 sums as equally likely. About 10 uses only one of the 6 ways to make 7.

items.q: You spin both spinners 80 times. About how many times would you expect each outcome?
items.e: There are 8 equally likely outcomes, so each has probability 18. 80 ÷ 8 = about 10. About 13 comes from 80 ÷ 6 (adding 2 + 4 outcomes).

items.q: The theoretical probability of two heads is 0.25. Group A tosses two coins 20 times and gets HH 8 times. Group B tosses them 400 times and gets HH 96 times. Whose experimental probability is closer to 0.25?
items.e: Group A: 820 = 0.4. Group B: 96400 = 0.24. 0.24 is much closer to 0.25, so Group B’s is closer.

items.q: Why are the results of 400 trials usually closer to the theory than the results of 20 trials?
c: More trials usually get closer to the theory
Big experiments always match the theory exactly
The coins wear out after 20 tosses
items.e: With only a few trials, luck changes the results a lot. More trials usually get closer to the theoretical probability, but not exactly.

items.q: Dennis tosses two coins 10 times and gets HH 4 times. He says the coins must be unfair because 0.4 is not 0.25. Is he right?
c: Yes, HH should come up exactly 2.5 times
No, 10 trials are too few to tell
No, HH can never come up 4 times
items.e: With only 10 trials, results can be far from the theory just by chance. 10 trials are too few to tell. He should do many more trials.

items.q: Two coins are tossed 1,000 times and HH comes up 381 times. What do the results suggest?
c: HH will now come up less often
1,000 trials are too few to tell
The coins are probably not fair
items.e: Theory: 14 of 1,000 = 250. 381 is far from 250 after a lot of trials, so the coins are probably not fair.

items.q: The experimental probability of an outcome is 0.3 and the theoretical probability is 0.25. What is the difference?
items.e: 0.30 − 0.25 = 0.05. 0.55 adds them instead of subtracting.

items.q: The theoretical probability of heads and an even number is 14. Which experimental result is closest to the theory?
items.e: As decimals: 0.26, 0.4, 0.35 and 0.5. 14 = 0.25, so 26 out of 100 is closest.

items.q: As the number of trials grows, which number is the experimental probability getting close to?
items.e: 0.35, 0.29, 0.26, 0.252 … the results get closer and closer to 0.25, the theoretical probability 14.

items.q: Two fair coins have landed TT four times in a row. What is the probability of HH on the next toss?
items.e: Coins have no memory. Every toss is a new trial, so HH is still 14. Thinking HH is “due” is called the gambler’s fallacy.

items.q: Andrea tosses a coin and gets heads. Then she rolls a number cube. What is the probability that the number cube shows a 6?
items.e: The coin does not change the number cube: the events are independent. A 6 is still 16. 112 is the chance of heads AND 6 before anything is tossed.

items.q: In 50 trials with a coin and a spinner, Kenneth gets heads and red 9 times. Use his results to predict how many times he will get heads and red in 200 trials.
items.e: 200 trials is 4 times as many as 50, so expect about 4 × 9 = 36. About 159 adds 150 instead of multiplying. About 18 only doubles.

items.q: You spin a red, blue and yellow spinner (3 equal sections) twice, and do this 90 times. About how many times would you expect both spins to be the same color?
items.e: P(same color) = 39 = 13. 13 of 90 = about 30. About 10 counts only one color. About 45 uses 36.

items.q: Which is the best way to make an experimental probability closer to the theoretical probability?
c: Use a new coin for each toss
Stop when the results look right
items.e: Results from a few trials vary a lot. Doing many more trials usually brings the experimental probability closer to the theory.

items.q: Why might a class use a computer simulation instead of tossing real coins?
c: It always matches the theory exactly
It can run thousands of trials quickly
items.e: A simulation can run thousands of trials quickly. With so many trials, the experimental probability usually gets close to the theory, but it is still not exact.

items.q: Emmanuel tosses a coin and rolls a number cube 120 times. He gets heads and an odd number 33 times. How does this compare with the theory?
items.e: Heads and odd: H1, H3, H5, so 312 = 14. 14 of 120 = 30. 33 is close to 30. About 60 uses heads only.

items.q: You toss a coin and spin this spinner 80 times. About how many times would you expect heads and red?
items.e: P(heads and red) = 12 × 34 = 38. 80 ÷ 8 × 3 = about 30. About 20 treats red and blue as equally likely. About 100 adds the probabilities (54).

items.q: In a game, you win if two coins match (HH or TT). Ana plays 100 times and wins 47 times. Do her results fit the theory?
c: Yes, 47 is close to the 50 the theory predicts
No, 47 means the game is unfair
No, she should win exactly 50 times
items.e: P(match) = 24 = 12, so theory predicts about 50 wins. 47 is close to 50; small differences are normal.
